# Chasing Down Kubernetes Ghosts with Humanlog

I was just here minding my own business, trying to setup the [CNPG operator](https://cloudnative-pg.github.io) in my [Tilt](https://tilt.dev/) environment:

```starlark
def main():
    setup_external_secrets()
    setup_ingress_nginx()
    install_cnpg_operator()
    install_cnpg_cluster("temporal-default")
    install_cnpg_cluster("temporal-visibility")

def install_cnpg_operator():
    # helm repo add cnpg https://cloudnative-pg.github.io/charts
    k8s_yaml(helm(
        './deploy/cnpg-operator',
        'cnpg-operator',
        namespace='default',
    ))

def install_cnpg_cluster(name):
    k8s_yaml(helm(
        './deploy/cnpg-clusters',
        'cnpg-clusters',
        namespace='default',
        values=[
            "./deploy/cnpg-clusters/values.yaml",
            "./deploy/cnpg-clusters/values-{name}.yaml".format(name=name),
        ]
    ))
```

And I couldn't for the life of me understand why Tilt was _sometimes_ failing to apply the YAML for the CNPG clusters (essentially Postgres):

```
Build Failed: Internal error occurred: failed calling webhook "mcluster.cnpg.io": failed to call webhook: Post "https://cnpg-webhook-service.default.svc:443/mutate-postgresql-cnpg-io-v1-cluster?timeout=10s": tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
```

Why is an error with `tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` showing up there? I'm not doing anything funky with TLS, it's a vanilla Kubernetes setup from [Orbstack](https://orbstack.dev/). And why is this setup working _sometimes_ but not always? Not knowing it's internals and transactional model, it's easy to assume that Titl might be getting in a weird state if I edit files too fast, so I turned down and up my local-dev environment multiple times and the error is inconsistent and shows up in various locations.

Anyways, I asked ChatGPT to help direct my search, and it told me to look into the `MutatingWebhookConfiguration` for the CNPG operator. Makes sense, matches the URL in the error string.

But, also I forgot what these mutating webhooks are about. My brain works like a cache, and mutating webhooks knowledge got evicted.

## Mutating Webhooks and Their Configuration

Per the Kubernetes docs:

> Admission webhooks are HTTP callbacks that receive admission requests and do something with them. You can define two types of admission webhooks, validating admission webhook and mutating admission webhook. Mutating admission webhooks are invoked first, and can modify objects sent to the API server to enforce custom defaults. After all object modifications are complete, and after the incoming object is validated by the API server, validating admission webhooks are invoked and can reject requests to enforce custom policies.
>
> - https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/

So somehow, there's a "mutating webhook server" listening on service `cnpg-webhook-service` for webhooks about `"mcluster.cnpg.io"`. And that server is returning a certificate signed with an authority unknown to the `kubectl` cliet (or Tilt's internal k8s client, not sure). Why is that?

Mutating webhooks are configured using a `mutatingwebhookconfiguration` object (so they say). In my case, this object looks like:

```bash
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration cnpg-mutating-webhook-configuration -o yaml
```

A configuration that enumerates multiple webhooks, and details about the way clients should invoke them (service name, namespace, path, port).

```yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: MutatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: cnpg-mutating-webhook-configuration
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: cnpg-operator
    app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: tilt
    app.kubernetes.io/name: cloudnative-pg
    app.kubernetes.io/version: 1.25.1
    helm.sh/chart: cloudnative-pg-0.23.2
webhooks:
  - admissionReviewVersions:
      - v1
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: cnpg-webhook-service
        namespace: default
        path: /mutate-postgresql-cnpg-io-v1-backup
        port: 443
    failurePolicy: Fail
    matchPolicy: Equivalent
    name: mbackup.cnpg.io
    namespaceSelector: {}
    objectSelector: {}
    reinvocationPolicy: Never
    rules:
      - apiGroups:
          - postgresql.cnpg.io
        apiVersions:
          - v1
        operations:
          - CREATE
          - UPDATE
        resources:
          - backups
        scope: "*"
    sideEffects: None
    timeoutSeconds: 10
  - admissionReviewVersions:
      - v1
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: cnpg-webhook-service
        namespace: default
        path: /mutate-postgresql-cnpg-io-v1-cluster
        port: 443
    failurePolicy: Fail
    matchPolicy: Equivalent
    name: mcluster.cnpg.io
    namespaceSelector: {}
    objectSelector: {}
    reinvocationPolicy: Never
    rules:
      - apiGroups:
          - postgresql.cnpg.io
        apiVersions:
          - v1
        operations:
          - CREATE
          - UPDATE
        resources:
          - clusters
        scope: "*"
    sideEffects: None
    timeoutSeconds: 10
  - admissionReviewVersions:
      - v1
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: cnpg-webhook-service
        namespace: default
        path: /mutate-postgresql-cnpg-io-v1-scheduledbackup
        port: 443
    failurePolicy: Fail
    matchPolicy: Equivalent
    name: mscheduledbackup.cnpg.io
    namespaceSelector: {}
    objectSelector: {}
    reinvocationPolicy: Never
    rules:
      - apiGroups:
          - postgresql.cnpg.io
        apiVersions:
          - v1
        operations:
          - CREATE
          - UPDATE
        resources:
          - scheduledbackups
        scope: "*"
    sideEffects: None
    timeoutSeconds: 10
```

In particular, we're looking at the `name: mcluster.cnpg.io` webhook, since that's what our error talks about (although we can assume the other webhooks probably suffer the same problem).

```
- admissionReviewVersions:
  - v1
  clientConfig:
    service:
      name: cnpg-webhook-service
      namespace: default
      path: /mutate-postgresql-cnpg-io-v1-cluster
      port: 443
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchPolicy: Equivalent
  name: mcluster.cnpg.io
  namespaceSelector: {}
  objectSelector: {}
  reinvocationPolicy: Never
  rules:
  - apiGroups:
    - postgresql.cnpg.io
    apiVersions:
    - v1
    operations:
    - CREATE
    - UPDATE
    resources:
    - clusters
    scope: '*'
  sideEffects: None
  timeoutSeconds: 10
```

When cross-referencing with the Kubernetes docs, notably missing here is the `caBundle` entry in the `clientConfig` children. The docs on this are clear:

> You must replace the `caBundle` in the above example by a valid CA bundle which is a PEM-encoded (field value is Base64 encoded) CA bundle for validating the webhook's server certificate.

We don't have a `caBundle` here and this seems like a problem, and it would make sense that we'd get `x509` errors from the pipes along the way if some client dialed a server without knowing that the server uses a specific certificate chain.

So why is this value not there? Is it _ever_ there? This is vanilla from the helm chart.

Let's pull the good old trick and turn it on and off again and see what's happening.

## Turning It Off And On Again

Let's tear down the environment with `tilt down` and bring it back up with `tilt up`. And then watch the webhook:

```bash
watch "kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration cnpg-mutating-webhook-configuration -o yaml | grep caBundle"
```

```
Error from server (NotFound): mutatingwebhookconfigurations.admissionregistration.k8s.io "cnpg-mutating-webhook-configuration" not found
```

And then we see:

```
Every 2.0s: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration cnpg-mutating-webhook-configuration -o yaml | grep caBundle                                                                                                orion.local: Tue Apr  1 16:38:46 2025
```

And silence. But when looking in Tilt's UI, the Postgres cluster didn't get created.

[!](/images/blog/debugging-k8s-audit-logs/tilt-on-coming-up.png)

Seems like Tilt tried to create the Postgres cluster _before_ the CNPG operator was done installing, so we trigger an update on the "uncategorized" group in which the error occured, and that's when we get the `x509` error:

```

Build Failed: Internal error occurred: failed calling webhook "mcluster.cnpg.io": failed to call webhook: Post "https://cnpg-webhook-service.default.svc:443/mutate-postgresql-cnpg-io-v1-cluster?timeout=10s": tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority

```

And then our watch terminal looks like this:
```

Every 2.0s: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration cnpg-mutating-webhook-configuration -o yaml | grep caBundle orion.local: Tue Apr 1 16:39:53 2025

````

The `caBundle` shows up and then disappears. Why?

Something is mutating the mutating webhook. Who?

## Kubernetes Audit Logs

The audit logs in Kubernetes are how you can figure out who touched what. The "who" can be a user, a controller, or the API server itself. And the "what" is Kubernetes resources.

> Kubernetes auditing provides a security-relevant, chronological set of records documenting the sequence of actions in a cluster. The cluster audits the activities generated by users, by applications that use the Kubernetes API, and by the control plane itself.
>
> Auditing allows cluster administrators to answer the following questions:
>
>     what happened?
>     when did it happen?
>     who initiated it?
>     on what did it happen?
>     where was it observed?
>     from where was it initiated?
>     to where was it going?
>
> - https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/audit/

In this case, we want to know "who" is touching our `kind: MutatingWebhookConfiguration`. By default, Kubernetes doesn't record audit logs. It needs a `kind: Policy` (`apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1`) to do anything of the sort. You can read more about this [in the reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/apiserver-audit.v1/#audit-k8s-io-v1-Policy).

In our case, the policy should include a `PolicyRule` that looks something like:

```yaml
- level: RequestResponse
  omitStages:
  - RequestReceived
  resources:
  - group: "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1"
    resources:
    - mutatingwebhookconfiguration
````

We want to know who's doing what to our mutating webhooks.

But it turns out that Orbstack doesn't allow customizing clusters in this manner, and the AuditPolicy of a cluster is a file that gets set on the filesystem of the API server of a Kubernetes cluster, and not via the API. So we need to fallback to another Kubernetes local-dev tool. My second favorite is [`kind`]()

## Configuring Audit Logs in Kind

We'll create a new Kubernetes cluster in kind and [turn on audit logging](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/auditing/) with this config (`kind-config.yaml`):

```yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    kubeadmConfigPatches:
      - |
        kind: ClusterConfiguration
        apiServer:
            # enable auditing flags on the API server
            extraArgs:
              audit-log-path: /var/log/kubernetes/kube-apiserver-audit.log
              audit-policy-file: /etc/kubernetes/policies/audit-policy.yaml
            # mount new files / directories on the control plane
            extraVolumes:
              - name: audit-policies
                hostPath: /etc/kubernetes/policies
                mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/policies
                readOnly: true
                pathType: "DirectoryOrCreate"
              - name: "audit-logs"
                hostPath: "/var/log/kubernetes"
                mountPath: "/var/log/kubernetes"
                readOnly: false
                pathType: DirectoryOrCreate
    # mount the local file on the control plane
    extraMounts:
      - hostPath: ./audit-policy.yaml
        containerPath: /etc/kubernetes/policies/audit-policy.yaml
        readOnly: true
```

And use this as our `audit-policy.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
  - level: None
    nonResourceURLs:
      - "/healthz*"
      - "/logs"
      - "/metrics"
      - "/swagger*"
      - "/version"

  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
      - group: "admissionregistration.k8s.io"
        resources:
          - mutatingwebhookconfigurations

  # log everything else at Metadata level
  - level: Metadata
    omitStages:
      - RequestReceived
```

If you're doing the same, note that you'll then have to run your cluster create command from the same path as where `audit-policy.yaml` is found, since we tell `kind` to find the file at a relative path on our host filesystem.

```
kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml
```

This creates a Kubernetes cluster that logs what's happening to everything at a `Metadata` level, and every `RequestResponse` about `mutatingwebhookconfiguration`.

But when we try to look at the logs:

```bash
docker exec kind-control-plane cat /var/log/kubernetes/kube-apiserver-audit.log
```

We just get an offensive amount of JSON logs.

## Bringing The Data In Humanlog

Offensive amount of JSON logs. That's exactly what `humanlog` is good at. Let's shove it into `humanlog` and continue our search from there.

```
docker exec kind-control-plane tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/kube-apiserver-audit.log | humanlog
```

And then we search for audit logs that match the mutatingwebhookconfigurations and involve an update or a delete:

```
filter ['objectRef.resource']=="mutatingwebhookconfigurations"
| filter (verb == "delete"  or verb == "patch")
| filter stage != "RequestReceived"
```

We get this result:

```
Apr 3 14:22:22.596 |RequestResponse| no message requestObject.webhooks.1.name=mcluster.cnpg.io auditID=b8060f91-dbd0-4a21-9142-45989f199498 requestObject.webhooks.2.matchPolicy=Equivalent annotations.authorization.k8s.io/reason=RBAC: allowed by ClusterRoleBinding "cnpg-operator-cloudnative-pg" of ClusterRole "cnpg-operator-cloudnative-pg" to ServiceAccount We can see that Tilt is deleting the `mutatingwebhookconfigurations` whenever I click the "trigger update" button. That's annoying.

## The Boring Reveal

It turns out that when I clicked the "trigger update" button of the shared "unrecognized" resource, with the intent of retrying to create the Postgres cluster, I also caused Tilt to _recreate the CNPG mutating webhook_.

[!](/images/blog/debugging-k8s-audit-logs/tilt-deleting-our-stuff.png)

And since Tilt doesn't know about the inter-dependency (I didn't tell it about it), it happily did both things at the same time, leading to the creation of the Postgres cluster to occur while the webhook was not yet provisioned with a `caBundle`. The solution? Tell Tilt about the dependency, make it group the Postgres cluster in its own block, and make the CNPG webhook join the resource group of the other CNPG components.

That's it!

## Conclusion

These investigations are often caused by [dumb PEBCAK errors](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/PEBCAK) (like here!), and the tools required to debug them can be complex. Debugging what's going on inside a local-dev install of Kubernetes is technically possible, but painful. In production, our Kubernetes cluster hopefully sends its audit logs to an observability pipeline (like Humanlog's!). But when it comes to local-dev, we're on our own with grep, tail, jq and patience. These are powerful tool, but when it comes to logs, so is humanlog. And all the research you can do in production can now be done in your local dev environment as well.

Give humanlog a try next time you're trying to debug your distributed system in local dev.
